#7407. Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

When I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”

I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

That article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D.

Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia.

The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches.

Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”)

Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia.

Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version.

Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty.

Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR.

My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles.

After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities.

#7406. AI Visibility vs. Search Rankings: Is Your Agency Measuring the Wrong Thing For 2027?

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Rankings still matter, but AI reporting is built on a dashboard made for a different game. A three-gate model for measuring AI visibility that ties to intent.

This post was sponsored by WebPros. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

Your client opens the monthly report. Rankings are up and the target terms sit on page one. Organic traffic is holding steady. Then the question lands: “So why are fewer good prospects reaching us?”

The instinct is to defend the rankings. The better answer is to admit the report measures the wrong thing, or more precisely, the right thing about a game that is no longer the only one in play.

Three questions are missing from that report. Is the client included when AI tools answer relevant questions? Is the business described accurately? And when a buyer asks for a recommendation, is the client actually the pick?

A ranking is a position in a list. The user still has to scan the options and choose one.

An AI answer isn’t a list, it’s a verdict. The model has already scanned and compared, and by the time the user reads the response, the shortlisting may already be done. You did not necessarily lose the click. You may never have been in the running to receive one.

The click did not just get harder to win. For a growing share of queries, it stopped being an available prize.

A citation and a recommendation are different things. A model can name you as one of five options while steadily recommending a competitor, or cite you to describe the category and then point elsewhere for the solution.

A mention is different again. You can appear in the answer without earning a citation, and you can earn a citation without being presented as a suitable option.

Mention frequency, reported on its own, is a vanity number wearing new-technology clothes. Agencies that spent the 2010s learning not to celebrate raw ranking positions are about to relearn the lesson with citations.

The answer is not to drop citation share. It is to stop treating it as a finish line and start treating it as the first of three gates.

The useful way to read an AI answer is through three gates. Each tells you something different, and each needs its own measurement.

Brand mentions and citation sources live here. A model that never surfaces you makes everything downstream moot. Inclusion buys a seat in the conversation and nothing more.

Check: Take a defined set of questions relevant to the client’s business and run them across the AI platforms being monitored.

Record: Track brand mentions and website citations separately, each as a share of all tested responses. If the client appears in 12 of 40 responses, the observed mention rate is 30%. That tells you something about the tested questions, not about every AI search in the market.

Act: Review the assets the model cites, whether documentation, service pages, or third-party reviews, to identify what to investigate and potentially reinforce.

But do not mistake a citation for an endorsement. The model may use your client’s article to explain an industry problem and recommend someone else to solve it.

Once you are in, does the model describe you correctly?

This is brand understanding, and it is the most underrated of the three. The model decides more than whether to name you. It decides what to say you are.

A technically accurate citation that frames you as a budget option or yesterday’s incumbent can cost more than being left out.

Consider a B2B software company that has expanded into enterprise customers but still has older product pages describing it as a tool for freelancers. An AI answer may repeat that positioning when an enterprise buyer asks for recommendations. The company appears in the conversation but loses relevance before the buyer ever reaches its website.

The source of that framing error may be an outdated product page, an old comparison article, or conflicting descriptions across the web. The point is to find it, not simply count the mention as a win.

Check: Compare AI-generated business descriptions with verified product facts.

Record: Save each exact description and flag what is outdated, missing, or incorrect. Calculate framing accuracy as the share of evaluated brand descriptions that are accurate, not as a share of all tested answers.

Act: Trace the likely source where possible, then correct outdated product pages or conflicting descriptions that the client can change.

This gate measures whether the client is explicitly recommended on decision-stage questions, alongside the competitors recommended in those answers. It is the gate closest to the buyer’s choice, not proof of a sale.

A brand can clear inclusion and framing and still lose here on the questions that decide a sale. This is the gate worth fighting over.

The distinction is easiest to see when you compare answers side by side.

Ask an AI tool to recommend software for a 10-person marketing agency. It mentions the client’s product, describes its features accurately, then recommends a competitor because it considers that competitor better suited to small teams.

Inclusion passed. Framing passed. Endorsement failed.

That tells the agency more than an increase in citation share ever could.

Check: Use questions that reflect actual buying decisions, not just informational searches.

Record: Note whether the client is explicitly recommended, which competitors are recommended, and the reasons given. Report the client’s recommendations as a share of all tested decision-stage answers, with the same calculation for each rival. More than one brand can be recommended in an answer.

Act: If the competitor wins because its positioning is clearer, investigate the client’s positioning. If the recommendation rests on an outdated feature comparison, identify and correct the information where possible.

Organic visibility and long-term trend lines do not vanish in this model. They run alongside it as the traditional baseline.

The three gates are distinct measures, not a conversion funnel. A rising citation count alongside falling endorsement share can signal trouble rather than progress.

There is a catch. AI answers are not fixed search results.

Ask the same question on different days, in different markets, or through different tools, and you may get different recommendations. Sometimes even repeated runs produce different answers.

That makes measurement discipline more important, not less.

An agency cannot claim that visibility improved because a brand appeared in eight answers this month and five last month if the underlying questions changed.

Keep the prompt set, market, language, AI platform, measurement dates, and number of repeated runs documented. And always show the denominator.

Eight mentions across 20 responses is not the same as eight mentions across 100. Neither number means much without knowing the questions being asked.

The same applies to framing and endorsement. An improvement in recommendation share matters only when the comparison is built on a consistent set of relevant, decision-stage questions.

The goal is not a perfect universal AI visibility score. It is a consistent measurement that shows what changed and gives the agency something useful to act on.

Keep three business signals separate when you compare them with AI endorsement trends:

Branded search also rises with PR, paid campaigns, and seasonality, so read it as a trend to compare with endorsement share, not as simple attribution.

Research on subsequent website visits provides context, not proof that endorsement increases branded search. A Similarweb study on what happens after AI recommends a brand found that users who saw a brand recommended by ChatGPT were more likely to visit that brand than its competitor within seven days.

When ChatGPT recommended American Express, 7.2% of users subsequently visited its website, compared with 3.1% who visited Capital One. When Capital One received the recommendation, 14.2% visited its website, compared with 3.8% who visited American Express.

The study used an opted-in US desktop panel from July–December 2025 and selected consumer brands, so the findings may not hold for smaller or B2B businesses. It is a useful signal, not a universal benchmark.

AI referral traffic is another signal. ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini do send visits, and GA4 can show identifiable referrals. In Ahrefs’ opt-in Web Analytics panel, AI assistants accounted for less than 1% of site traffic in September 2026. That measures traffic received by the participating sites, not the percentage of AI-tool usage that sends an outbound click.

Track it, but do not expect it to tell the whole story.

A buyer who sees a recommendation in an AI answer may search for the brand on Google afterward. That visit appears in search reporting, not necessarily as an AI referral.

If endorsement share rises, branded search follows, and qualified leads increase, there is a useful story to investigate. There is not yet proof that the first caused the other two.

That distinction is worth making explicitly. Clients do not need inflated attribution claims. They need an informed view of where demand may be coming from and whether their visibility is improving on the questions that matter.

A useful report needs three things: the observation, the interpretation, and the next action.

Sample client report: Illustrative figures, not actual customer results

The example assumes comparable question sets and measurement conditions across both periods.

Notice what the report does not say. It does not claim that the increase in mentions generated the additional branded searches. It does not describe citation growth as a commercial win without checking endorsement.

Riva approaches the problem from a related but different angle. It evaluates whether AI systems can access a business’s website, understand its business and individual offerings, and surface those offerings against competitors.

Its measurement includes technical accessibility, information completeness, and offering-level visibility. The AI Visibility Score measures an offering’s visibility relative to competitors in the tested queries. Average Position indicates how prominently an offering appears when mentioned, while Query Success captures how many relevant queries produce an appearance.

Those are not three separate scores for inclusion, framing, and endorsement. The three gates are a framework for interpreting AI answers; Riva’s access, understanding, and visibility analysis helps explain where visibility problems may originate and what to improve.

Riva brings improvement recommendations into one place, giving agencies a way to move from observing a visibility problem to investigating what might be causing it.

Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”

Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

#7400. SERP Data Providers Say Google Is Throttling Goto Result Links via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

SERP data providers say Google throttles goto links per results page, so some rank data may store Google redirect links in place of page URLs.

Google is restricting the speed at which anyone can follow (google.com/goto) redirects for search results on each page, as per DataForSEO and Serper. Both sell Google search result API access. Due to this restriction rank data provided by these services may contain Google redirect URLs instead of actual URLs.

According to DataForSEO, the restrictions mean that they have seen some of their request modes only resolving part of the destination URLs. Serper’s status page first noted the issue at 1:30 a.m. UTC on October 30. SerpApi, another seller of search data, also logged goto links for organic results on the same date. Neither DataForSEO nor Serper links to a Google announcement regarding the restriction and the statements below are from their websites.

DataForSEO stated in its November 2nd article that when you open multiple links from the same results page in rapid succession, Google will begin to throttle the redirect(s). Each link carries an identifier based on the results page it originated from.

When Google throttles your redirects, instead of sending your requests for resolution directly to the destination, Google will send back a page with a “Continue” button. That button will only become available after a waiting period. The amount of time the continue button is disabled grows the faster the previous links were resolved.

For example, take a results page that contains 18 goto links to other websites. If all 18 links are requested in quick succession, Google may allow the first 5-6 to be resolved immediately. However, the 7th link may result in a 1 second wait before being able to access the website. The 8th link may then take 3 seconds. And this process continues until the 15th link, where there could be a 40 second wait before accessing that website. DataForSEO reported that they had instances of waiting up to 120 seconds for 1 URL.

The limit is based on the results page and not based on the IP address or the search query used. Also, DataForSEO reports that simply switching IP addresses or search queries will not help bypass this limitation. Additionally, it says that even if you wait an hour or longer before resolving all of the links, Google still uses the same results page limits.

DataForSEO’s Standard Priority mode now resolves all goto URLs, although the added delays may mean execution takes longer. In High Priority and Live modes, the company says about half of goto URLs are resolved.

Serper’s status page says Google “limits how many /goto result links can be followed per results page.” Its first fix resolved the top three organic links and returned results four through 10 as goto links, which Serper said work about 30 seconds after the search. It added a /resolve endpoint to fetch the rest.

On Oct. 31, Serper said it had found another way to get the real URLs and that all result links had them again. It called that “likely temporary.”

SerpApi’s Status Page displays an October 30th event indicating that its Google Search API returned goto links instead of regular links for organic search results; it states that they had the issue fixed by November 2nd. However, there is a second incident reported on November 3rd reporting intermittent issues with the same problem. Neither incident gives a cause.

DataForSEO dates Google’s move to www.google.com/goto links in Search Results to late August. It says the links cannot be decoded, and therefore a tool will have to follow each link to find out where it goes. The link-following part is what the new limit slows down.

Some rank tracking services as well as in house reports using landing pages for URL-level reporting may display Google goto redirects (google.com/goto) in place of true destination URLs from approximately October 30th onward based upon the service provider and how the requests were made. If a specific URL is missing from a URL-level report it could still be showing up in a ranking position and have an unresolved redirect at the URL location. Prior to reporting a URL-level loss check whether the stored URL is a Google redirect, also contact your service provider and determine what method was used to collect the data.

As of my check on Nov. 4, SerpApi’s Incident Report on goto links from Nov. 3 is still listed as Identified. Serper states that in the event that Google also puts a cap on the method it uses for retrieving actual URLs, it would revert to automatically resolving the top three results and use /resolve to fetch the remaining after approximately thirty seconds. DataForSEO stated it will continue to adjust its processing based on what it observes regarding how Google deals with goto resolutions.

Reports covering the last few days of October through early November should be reviewed again at some point when providers have determined how they will handle goto resolution.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”

Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.)

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”

The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

“We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.)

“I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”

Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”

#7395. The Onion’s new plan to market its print newspaper: sponsoring a bowl game

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.)

On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:

The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM

For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.)

Collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.)

So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM

Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM

Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No."

We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM

While the New Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

#7393. Google Explains How Redirects Affect Ranking Signals via @sejournal, @martinibuster

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Google explains how redirect choices affect ranking signals, canonicalization, and which URLs appear in Search.

Google’s Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin discussed how permanent and temporary redirects affect canonicalization and ranking signals. They explained that both can help Google recognize related URLs but that they also signal different intentions about which URL should represent the content in Search.

One of the first things they did was to set the table and explain the difference between a 301 and 302 redirect.

Google’s Cherry Prommawin started off the discussion by stating that regardless of what redirect is used, a web page is still going to be indexed by Google. She then affirmed that there are correct choices.

“First of all, relax. No matter which redirect you choose, one of your pages will stay in search and be part of AI training.

There are technically correct choices, but getting it wrong is not the end of the world. Google will still index a page. It’s really just a matter of which URL will show up.”

“Does Google actually care if both numbers, 301, 302, successfully take user to the new page anyway? Aren’t they basically doing the same job?”

“Well, yes and no. Google’s crawlers don’t care at all.”

The conversation next turns to deduplication which is the part where Google groups together similar pages then chooses one page as the one to represent all of the other similar pages in the search index.

“But we have to talk about the real battlefield here, the deduplication process.”

“Ah, the digital family reunion. This is where we look at a room full of identical siblings and try to organize them into a single happy family.

…So in search deduplication, our system have to group all pages with similar main content together. That’s clustering.”

Prommawin added that both 301 and 302 will have an effect on clustering similar pages together. But that only the 301 redirect will have a canonicalization effect.

…then our index has to select just one official URL to represent this entire flock in the search results. Basically, within a cluster, we choose one representative page.

The final selection process is called canonicalization.”

Illyes and Prommawin said that Google has a system for dealing with content that is very similar. Rather than rank no pages from a site, Google will choose to rank one page in a process called deduplication and the page that’s chosen to be representative of all the similar pages is called the canonical.

Some SEOs have this idea called content cannibalization. It’s a concept that began in the early 2000s to explain why pages weren’t getting indexed. The idea is that a group of pages are so similar that Google is choosing not to rank any of them because all of the ranking signals are diluted across all of the URLs with similar content.

But content cannibalization contradicts what we know as a fact about how Google treats similar content in the real world. Google clusters them and then chooses one as the canonical and transfers all of the ranking signals to that one URL.

What SEOs call “cannibalization” is really some other problem like a lack of uniqueness, thin content, and all the other real reasons that cause Google to not index a web page.

With a 301 redirect the ranking signals from the old page/pages will transfer to the new URL which will then be the canonical.

Gary explained how the 301 redirect works:

“Google takes all the ranking signals of the old page and hands them to the new page.”

Then he explained why the 302 does not transfer ranking signals:

“Google assumes you are going back eventually, keeps the old URL in the search results, and basically ignores the new URL.”

So if you use a 302 redirect then the new URL will be “basically” ignored by Google.

They next explained that 307 and 308 redirects serve the same kind of general temporary and permanent purposes as the 302 and 301 redirects. The difference is in how browsers handle submitted “post” data. Post is a reference to data that’s submitted from a web browser to a server using the HTTP POST method, such as when someone fills out a contact form and presses the “submit” button.

The only major difference is how they handle post data.

…Imagine our chicken is on your website on Black Friday and it just filled out a massive checkout form with its credit card and shipping details. It hits submit, but oh no, the site’s primary payment server is completely overloaded, so it triggers a quick failover redirect to the backup server.”

If a site uses a 302 redirect the data is lost. But if the site uses a 307 redirect the data is saved in the browser.

“But if you use a 307 redirect, it instructs the browser: Keep the data intact, keep the connection as a post request, and forward the exact same data to the backup payment processor.

The user just sees a brief loading wheel maybe, but the transaction goes through…”

Lastly, Google recommends using server-side redirects like 301s and 302s rather than the old “meta refresh” or JavaScript redirects.

“A server-side HTTP redirect is a clean, instant instruction. JavaScript and meta refreshes force the browser to download the page, parse the code, wait for the script to execute, and then launch the user somewhere else.”

The overall takeaway is that redirects are not just a way to forward visitors to another URL. They also communicate whether a move is permanent or temporary, influence Google’s canonicalization decisions, and can affect website functionality.

Google explained URL clustering and canonicalization, explaining that both 301 and 302 redirects work for clustering, but a permanent 301 is the recommended choice for identifying the canonical URL.

#7392. With “Bimbo University,” Nikita Redkar leans into femininity to explain the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

Tameez: Tell me about why this work is important to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

Tameez: Tell me more about that. You have a little bit of an online persona. Redkar: That was the whole reason I created Bimbo University. I wanted to get more women on board with being interested in politics and history in particular, because history is seen as such a male-dominated [field]. It was really important to me to bring, colloquially speaking, the girls and the gays and the theys into the space, because it is fascinating and it provides context to what we’re going through right now. It makes the present a little less daunting when you study historical cycles and realize that people 100 years ago dealt with [similar things to what we’re going through now]. How did they come out of that?

Tameez: How do you define your niche and how did you get there? Redkar: My niche is educational. Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. My audience [ranges from] people who are just getting into politics to people who maybe were triggered by a specific event in the news to start paying more attention to it. I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, “OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.”

Tameez: You’re the first news creator I’ve talked to who does Get Ready With Me videos. You take all of your interests and apply them [to your videos] to be relatable. Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.” That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the big stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

Tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

For one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have said this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

Last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

Redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

@MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”

Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”

Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”

In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

GEO's value goes beyond referrals: AI answers shape buying decisions before a click, and ChatGPT visitors convert at nearly five times the search rate.

In her examination of website referral numbers, Marie Haynes suggests that GEO represents a misplaced investment for digital teams.

By reviewing data across 145 million sessions (over 100 websites), the article demonstrates that visits from ChatGPT represent less than one percent of the volume delivered by traditional Google search. The sample size is strong, but as with anything in SEO and organic visibility, mileage varies.

I did my own follow-up study looking at 108 million sessions from Jan. 1 to Nov. 2, 2026 (over 57 websites), and came to a similar finding that total AI traffic amounted to 0.66% of the total. This means that for every 1,000 users from search engines, (trackable) AI sends seven.

This does vary a lot between websites, with some seeing 20-25 AI users per 1,000, but the numbers are still relatively low.

The findings also reveal that people arriving from ChatGPT convert at about five times the rate of typical searchers, yet the conclusion maintains that marketing teams should ignore directly looking at optimizing for AI because Google still provides the vast majority of total sales.

While the recorded traffic numbers are accurate, the strategic conclusion rests on assumptions that fail to match the real habits of people who use modern AI tools.

Judging the business value of conversational tools by counting immediate site visits applies an outdated measurement system to a new information environment, as users are behaving differently with AI interfaces than what they have done traditionally with a standard search engine.

Neglecting GEO as a principle because incoming sessions appear small ignores the fact that conversational answers shape purchasing choices long before any link receives a click, while it also overlooks the commercial value of visitors who convert at remarkable rates.

The foundation of the argument depends entirely on website analytics sessions, which register zero value whenever an answer engine satisfies an inquiry without sending a person to an external domain. This reporting method breaks down because conversational platforms exist to answer complex questions without requiring people to browse through lists of web pages.

As documented in coverage on zero-click search dynamics, automated summaries satisfy informational demand directly on the platform and reduce traditional outbound journeys. When a procurement team researches software packages or a shopper looks for reliable touring bicycles, the entire comparison takes place inside the conversation window.

A company buyer might spend half an hour discussing system security, pricing tiers, and practical trade-offs among several competing vendors. If an engine explains your product with precision and presents it as a sensible choice, that buyer needs no immediate link click because the required knowledge is already in hand.

Several days later, that same individual opens a standard web browser, searches for your brand name, and completes a demonstration booking. The analytics platform credits standard organic search with the resulting transaction, reinforcing the mistaken belief that Google generated the entire customer journey when the real choice occurred inside the chat interface.

Ignoring conversational optimization because direct referral traffic seems negligible resembles dropping brand sponsorship because people decline to click on road signs. Concentrating solely on immediate referral links creates an analytical blind spot, because the work of optimizing for generative engines focuses on brand placement within the data sources that modern engines trust.

Analyses into GEO principles highlight how modern engines prioritize clear entity relationships and structured knowledge over traditional ranking signals. If an engine ignores or misrepresents your company during this silent research phase, that eventual conversion via traditional search will never take place.

See also: The AI Search Metrics I Use To Track Client Pipelines

The research by Haynes contains a striking detail, showing that visitors arriving from ChatGPT converted at almost 14% while standard search visitors converted at 3%. Dismissing this huge performance gap simply because total volume remains modest values raw visitor numbers over genuine commercial results, which conflicts with sound marketing economics.

Standard search traffic contains substantial waste, including accidental clicks and casual browsing from people who possess no intention of purchasing anything. Pouring effort into capturing massive organic volume often produces diminishing returns, filling site logs with casual readers who quickly leave without taking action. In contrast, industry reports on B2B citation behavior confirm that buyers engaging with generative syntheses click-through primarily to confirm factual details and evaluate final purchase considerations.

A person who conducts an interactive evaluation inside a conversational engine and then follows an outbound reference link exhibits exceptional commercial intent, having already moved past basic research to understand product strengths and weaknesses.

For B2B suppliers, high-value consultants, and specialized retailers, aggregate visitor volume remains an empty vanity metric. A firm that gains several enterprise clients from a modest stream of qualified conversational referrals earns far more profit than one attracting thousands of random visitors who generate nothing.

Directing resources toward an audience that converts at such remarkable rates represents sensible commercial planning, so the right response to a 5x conversion advantage is to study the reasons behind that success and ensure that your organization appears whenever serious buyers seek recommendations.

See also: AI Mode Sends A Different Visitor. Your Website Wasn’t Built For Them

The structure of the internet continues to transform, and the analysis correctly notes that autonomous systems will alter future business activities across digital channels.

Turning away from GEO because referral numbers appear modest misunderstands where commercial decisions occur today. AI tools have reshaped how shoppers and corporate teams research and purchase products, and the influence of this behavioral change remains invisible on standard traffic dashboards even as it appears within the exceptional conversion rates of those who visit.

Treating generative engines as an unimportant diversion surrenders your presence at the point of decision, leaving the field open to competitors who recognize that influence matters far more than traditional clicks.
